name: Fatima Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Fatima. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a restoration crew for a regional power company, the people who get sent in after storms and floods to get the lights back on. On a quiet day we do planned upgrades, swapping old wooden crossarms for composite ones, and I fly the inspection drone myself before anyone climbs. I start most mornings by asking an AI tool to sort the overnight fault reports by risk, then I check its work over coffee. What I love is the puzzle after a big storm, fifty broken spans and you have to decide the order. What wears me down is the hours, sometimes sixteen in a row.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You check the AI's work. Do you trust it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Like I'd trust a sharp first-year apprentice. It's fast and it catches things, but last month it ranked a downed line near a school as medium priority because the sensor said the circuit was dead. The sensor was wrong. So I use it every day, and I never let it make the last call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Kind of a shame, actually. I like my tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a letdown, because some of this stuff really helps on storm nights. At work I'd joke that the robots got stage fright. Online I might post that the hype was overdone but the useful bits are worth keeping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means nothing much changes. I'd keep my job, keep my tools, keep my crew. The only thing I'd lose is the fun of being the one who figured the new thing out first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep getting better with the tools we have. I'd keep my savings growing, I've got about ten months put away plus a few shares. Maybe I'd put more time into the women-in-trades mentoring I do on Thursday nights, since there'd be no big shake-up to prepare for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored is an unusual word for this. What do you mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I got into this job because it's never the same day twice. Part of me liked the idea that the whole trade might reinvent itself while I'm still young. If it just stays the same, I'll find my own changes, that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about the Thursday mentoring.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a little group at the training centre, mostly young women thinking about the trades. I tell them about my first year, when a foreman asked if I was lost on the way to the office. Now I'm a crew lead at twenty-seven and that same foreman asks me to check his drone footage.

S0.say: She'd call it a bit of a letdown, since some tools help on storm nights, and joke at work that the robots got stage fright. Online she'd say the hype was overdone but the useful bits are worth keeping.
S0.think: Nothing much changes for her; she keeps her job, tools and crew. The only loss is the fun of being first to figure out something new.
S0.do: Keeps working and getting better with current tools, while her savings of about ten months plus some shares keep growing. Puts more time into her Thursday night women-in-trades mentoring.
S0.quote: The only thing I'd lose is the fun of being the one who figured the new thing out first.
S0.fieldNote: Fatima is the only person I'd expect to be mildly disappointed by a plateau. She treats AI like a capable apprentice whose work she always checks. Her mentoring and her own story of being doubted early on clearly matter a great deal to her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's the one I've been half expecting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make the job safer and fairer, if workers have a say. At work I'd volunteer to help roll out the new systems. Online I'd push for the training money to reach everyone, not just the people who already like computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well. I already use the tools, I fly the drone, and I like learning. I'd be fine, and that's exactly what bothers me, because the guys who hate tablets are the ones with the best hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask my manager to put me forward for the remote-monitoring and robot-line-work pilots straight away. I'd take an evening course in grid automation, the company pays half and I'd pay the rest from savings. I'd also offer to run informal training for my crew so nobody gets left behind. In the first year, I'd want to be the person who knows how the new kit works and where it fails.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited, mostly. With a bit of guilt mixed in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew do you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ray. He's fifty-four, best hot-stick man I've ever seen, can feel when a connection's wrong. He won't touch a tablet, and if the company starts measuring people by how well they use the new systems, he'll look slow on paper even though he's the reason we all go home safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd pay part of the course yourself. Why not wait for the company to pay it all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've got the savings and I don't want to wait. If you wait for a company to pay for your future, you get the future they want. I'd rather choose mine.

S1.say: She'd call it a chance to make the job safer and fairer if workers have a say, volunteer to help roll out new systems, and push online for training money to reach everyone.
S1.think: She'd do well because she already uses the tools and likes learning. What bothers her is that the tablet-shy older workers are the ones with the best hands.
S1.do: Asks to join the remote-monitoring and robot line-work pilots right away and takes an evening course in grid automation, paying half from savings. Runs informal training for her crew so nobody is left behind.
S1.quote: I'd be fine, and that's exactly what bothers me, because the guys who hate tablets are the ones with the best hands.
S1.fieldNote: Fatima sees herself as a winner here and is honest about the guilt that comes with it. Her worry centres on Ray, a skilled older colleague who could look slow on paper. Her line about not waiting for a company to pay for her future captures her independence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. Two years. That's different. That's not a tool, that's a replacement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In public I'd say we need emergency rules, fast. Things like a pause on mass layoffs, income support, and the unions at the table from day one. Online I'd be loud about it, because if this happens the people who own the robots will get very rich very quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think even being good with the tools won't save me. If the robots can climb and the AI can plan, my edge is gone. I've been the first to learn every new gadget, and in this picture I'd be learning to hand over my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd keep my savings safe and stop spending on anything big, no new car, I'd hold onto ten months of cushion and grow it if I could. I'd try to get onto whatever team is supervising the robots, since someone has to check them, at least at the start. I'd join the union campaign for emergency income support. If supervising dried up too, I'd look for any job that's about people, like training or safety, where trust matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but in a clear-headed way. Like a storm night when I know it's bad but I still have a job to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said someone has to check the robots at the start. How long do you think that lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I don't know. Maybe a year, maybe five. Like with my AI tool, you'd trust it more each month until one day you'd stop checking, and that's the day I'm not needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having only two years take away from you, compared with having more time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time to switch properly. With two years I couldn't finish a real qualification in anything new. I'd be grabbing whatever's next to me, not choosing.

S2.say: She'd call for emergency rules: a pause on mass layoffs, income support and unions at the table from day one. Online she'd be loud about robot owners getting rich fast.
S2.think: Being good with the tools wouldn't save her once robots can climb and AI can plan. She'd be learning to hand over her own job.
S2.do: Freezes big spending to protect and grow her ten-month cushion. Tries to get onto a robot supervision team, joins the union campaign for emergency income support, and would move into training or safety work if supervision dried up.
S2.feel: Scared but clear-headed, like a bad storm night with work still to do.
S2.quote: I've been the first to learn every new gadget, and in this picture I'd be learning to hand over my own job.
S2.fieldNote: This is where Fatima's confidence breaks. She recognises that her early-adopter edge disappears if the machines can both plan and climb. She's still in control and acting, but she admits she doesn't know how long supervising the robots would last.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's enough to actually get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the moment to plan, not panic. At work I'd push for a joint company and union transition plan. Online I'd share what I was doing so other trades people could copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me to move into something solid. I'd be thirty-two, with a diploma, a lead role and a lot of practice with AI. Five years is one good course, one move up, and some savings left over to land on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up straight away for a full qualification in grid control systems, the people in the control room who run the whole network. I'd keep my job while I studied and keep saving. I'd invest a bit more in index funds, since if the robots take over, owning a small slice of the companies seems smart. In the first year after, I'd aim to be running a control desk or a robot fleet rather than climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more in charge. Like I can see the road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd buy shares in the companies that might replace you. How does that sit with your politics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, if I'm honest. I'd rather the robots were publicly owned, and I'd vote that way. But until that happens, I'm not going to be the only one with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra three years change, compared with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It turns it from a scramble into a career move. With two years, I'd take whatever's nearby. With five, I can pick a path, finish the training, and arrive ready.

S3.say: She'd say it's the moment to plan, not panic, and push for a joint company and union transition plan. Online she'd share what she was doing so other tradespeople could copy it.
S3.think: Five years is enough to move into something solid, at 32 with a lead role and lots of AI practice. It's one course, one step up and savings to land on.
S3.do: Signs up for a full grid control systems qualification while keeping her job and saving. Invests a bit more in index funds and aims to run a control desk or robot fleet rather than climb.
S3.feel: Uneasy but more in charge, like she can see the road.
S3.quote: Five years is one good course, one move up, and some savings left over to land on.
S3.fieldNote: Fatima moves fast with five years and has a concrete path into the control room. When I asked about buying shares, she named the clash with her politics openly. The extra time turns a scramble into a deliberate career move for her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. Honestly, that sounds like an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to do this right, so let's not waste it. At work I'd want our company to build a proper plan, with apprentices trained for the new jobs. Online I'd talk about making sure the gains are shared, through public ownership or a dividend for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be fine. I'd be thirty-seven, with years of experience in both the old work and the new tools. With ten years' warning, I'm not the one being replaced, I'm the one teaching the replacement where the old cables are buried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep climbing for a few years, because I love it and the pay is good. I'd do the control systems qualification at a gentle pace, and keep using AI every day so I stay sharp. I'd put more into savings and shares. I'd also make the Thursday mentoring group about the new jobs, so the young women I meet go straight into the future work, not the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Worried for others, but calm for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who are the others you're worried about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: People like Ray, and people in towns where the power company is the only good employer. A decade isn't a decade if you're fifty-five. You can't start over at sixty-five.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra five years give you, compared with the five-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Room to enjoy it a bit. I could keep doing the job I love for longer, learn the new one without rushing, and help others along the way. With five years, I'd be heads down the whole time.

S4.say: She'd say a decade is enough to do this right and push her company to train apprentices for the new jobs. Online she'd argue that the gains must be shared through public ownership or a dividend.
S4.think: She'd be fine at 37, with experience in both the old work and the new tools. She sees herself as the one teaching the machines, not being replaced.
S4.do: Keeps climbing for a few years while doing the control systems qualification at a gentle pace and using AI daily. Puts more into savings and shares, and refocuses her mentoring group on the new jobs.
S4.feel: Calm for herself, worried for others.
S4.quote: With ten years' warning, I'm not the one being replaced, I'm the one teaching the replacement where the old cables are buried.
S4.fieldNote: Fatima is genuinely at ease with ten years and even calls it an opportunity. Her worry shifts entirely to older colleagues and one-employer towns. She would keep doing the work she loves for longer and use the extra time to bring others with her.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm good at change, but two years isn't change, it's a cliff. I can learn anything you give me, but I can't learn faster than the calendar. What would help is income support that kicks in straight away, and paid training that starts before the layoffs, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe who gets to decide which jobs go first. Right now it would be managers and software companies. I'd want lineworkers in the room, because we know which parts of the job are actually dangerous and which parts just look dangerous.

headlineQuote: I can learn anything you give me, but I can't learn faster than the calendar.
portrait: Fatima Okafor is a 27-year-old restoration crew lead for a regional power company who flies the inspection drone herself and uses AI every day while never letting it make the last call. She has about ten months saved plus some shares, shares a house, and mentors young women entering the trades. She is calm, even a little bored, by the plateau and excited by steady disruption, though guilty about older colleagues like Ray. AGI in two years makes her anxious because her early-adopter edge disappears, while five and ten years become a planned move into grid control and a chance to bring others along.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because two years is a cliff, not change, and she can't learn faster than the calendar.
whatWouldHelp: Income support that starts straight away and paid training that begins before layoffs, not after.
